## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The book presents itself as Government Analysis Function guidance, produced by the Analysis Standards and Pipelines hub of the Office for National Statistics, that "describes software engineering good practices that are tailored to those working with data using code"; its stated purpose is to help readers quality assure their code and increase the reproducibility of their analyses, and it calls software that applies these practices reproducible analytical pipelines (RAP) [V] (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book"). It is language agnostic, gives examples in Python and R because those open-source languages are common across government, and says it does not aim to be a comprehensive learning resource [AP] (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book"). Each chapter describes the risks a practice may help address, and, following the Aqua book, readers should "strive to apply the most appropriate and proportionate quality assurance practices given the risks associated with your work" [V] (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book").

The argument rests on three founding principles of good analysis, each supported by the one before it: reproducible, auditable and assured; programming makes each easier to fulfil "in most cases" [AR] (book/principles.md, "Principles"). Analysis must be fit for purpose, because "Bad analysis can result in harm or misallocation of public funds." [V] (book/principles.md, "Principles"). Reproducibility is placed first and above the rest: "Reproducibility is the only thing that you can guarantee in your analysis." [V] and the further assurances of peer review, rigorous testing and validity are called "secondary" to being able to reproduce an analysis in a proportionate amount of time [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). The book sets this against manual or semi-manual production with proprietary tools and office software, a process it calls prone to error "because the input data and the outputs are not connected directly, only through the analyst’s manual intervention" [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines").

The chapters turn the principles into practices: modular and readable code, project structure, code and project documentation, version control, configuration, data management, peer review, testing and automation. The frame behind them is stated in the readable-code chapter: "when we write code for analysis, we are developing software" [V], so analysts can benefit from at least partially applying the good practices software engineering teams have developed [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Software ideas for analysts"). Proportionality recurs across the guidance: managers agree a target assurance level with their team, should not need to read the code to trust it, and where code assurance falls short of the target they supplement it with more in-depth assurance of outputs such as dual running [AR] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk").

The last chapter, marked a work in progress, extends the guidance to large language models used as coding assistants ("vibe coding"). It explains LLMs as next-word predictors built on neural networks, says hallucinations are "mathematically inevitable" [V], sets three "golden rules" (review any LLM-generated code yourself before using it or submitting it to peer review, you alone are responsible for it, never put sensitive information into a chatbot), weighs cited evidence on productivity and risk, and closes on Cory Doctorow's centaur and reverse-centaur framing with a worked CoPilot example [AR] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"; "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs").

## Part I: Purpose, audience and status of the book

### What the book is for and who it serves

The guidance is relevant to people who write code to automate part of their work, develop statistical or data engineering pipelines, develop models, develop data science techniques, or want a high-level introduction to software engineering practices for analysis and research [AP] (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book"). The practices are general to many applications of programming, so they may be relevant outside government too [AP] (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book"). The RAP learning pathway provides training for many of the practices; the book is meant to guide learning and to serve as a reference when applying them [AP] (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book").

The hub "supports government analysis by providing guidance, consultancy and training" [V] (book/intro.md, "About us"). "The guidance is a living document, which is continually updated." [V] (book/intro.md, "Quality assurance of code for analysis and research"). The book's versions use a form of calendar versioning: the first four digits give the year of the latest changes and the number after the full stop counts the versions published that year [AP] (book/project_documentation.md, "Versioning"). The suggested citation names version 2026.1 [V] (book/intro.md, "Citing the book").

The licence summary: readers may use, adapt and distribute the information with citation but may not imply endorsement, and the information is provided "'as is' without warranty" [V] (book/intro.md, "Citing the book"). The accessibility statement says the website is managed by the Quality and Improvement division of the ONS, excludes referenced third-party content and says users should be able to change colours, contrast levels and fonts, zoom up to 300% without text spilling off the screen, navigate most of the website using a keyboard or speech-recognition software, and listen to most of the website using a screen reader, describes keyboard navigation, commits to aim to respond to accessibility requests within five working days, and names the Equality and Human Rights Commission as the enforcing body under the 2018 public sector accessibility regulations [AP] (book/intro.md, "Accessibility statement"; "Help us improve this book"; "Enforcement procedure").

### Glossary

The glossary defines terms used through the book [AP] (book/glossary.md, "Terms"). Definitions that carry the book's own positions:

- *Code interpreter.* A non-interactive interpreter runs code in order, "which is important for reproducibility" [V]; interactive interpreters, which notebooks use, let code run out of order and are not suitable for running analysis pipelines [AP] (book/glossary.md, "Code interpreter").
- *Dual Running.* "In a RAP context, where a pipeline or process is run in different ways, on different systems, or by different people to verify reproducibility." [V] (book/glossary.md, "Dual Running").
- *Notebooks.* Used to share exploratory results, but because parts can run out of order "they are not suitable for production of published outputs" [V] (book/glossary.md, "Notebooks").
- *Open source.* The book recommends Python and R; it calls SPSS, SAS and Stata closed source, "expensive to use" and not supporting many of the book's good practices, so users would have to buy software to reproduce results [V] (book/glossary.md, "Open source").
- *Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAP).* Analyses carried out following the good software engineering practices the guidance describes, focused on open-source tools and techniques for "reproducible, auditable, and assured" analyses; "RAP is more generally a culture of wanting to improve the quality of our analysis, by improving the quality assurance of our analysis code." [V] (book/glossary.md, "Reproducible Analytical Pipelines (RAP)").
- *Maintainability* is the "Ability to easily understand, modify and repair the code."; *Readability* is the "Ability to gain an understanding of code within a reasonable amount of time." [V] (book/glossary.md, "Maintainability"; "Readability").
- *Peer review* helps assure code is readable and follows a sensible approach and transfers understanding of the code within the team [AP] (book/glossary.md, "Peer review").
- Other entries define abstraction, API, attribute, automated testing, class, cloud computing, code, code repository, configuration file, CI/CD, debugger, dependencies, documentation, functions and methods, Git, instance, IDE, "Interative Running", logging, modularity, module, OOP, packages, parameters and arguments, pipeline, procedural running, program, Python and R, scripts, variables, version control, version control platforms and virtual environments [AP] (book/glossary.md, "Terms").

## Part II: Principles of good analysis

### Three founding principles

The book "recognises three founding principles of good analysis, each supported by the one before it" [V], shown in the figure "Founding principles of good analysis" [AP] (book/principles.md, "Principles"). Reproducibility "guarantees that we have done what we are claiming to have done, and that others can easily replicate our work"; auditability means knowing why the analysis was chosen and who is responsible for each part, including assurance; assurance "improves the average quality and includes the communication of that quality to users" [V] (book/principles.md, "Principles").

A "Key strategies" box recommends five pieces of government guidance (the Analysis Function RAP strategy, the Aqua book, the Analysis Function Quality Strategy, the DCMS Data Ethics Framework, and the Communicating quality, uncertainty and change guidance) and says "Each of these pieces of guidance advocate reproducibility as a core tenet of quality analysis." [V] (book/principles.md, "Principles").

### Reproducible

Reproducibility is "the first pillar of good analysis" [V]. "If you can't prove that you can run the same analysis, with the same data, and obtain the same results, then you are not adding a valuable analysis." [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). A reproducible, transparent process lets anyone follow the steps, eases reuse, helps colleagues test and validate, and frees users and colleagues to focus on verifying that the implementation is correct and the research useful [AP] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). Reproducibility relies on effective documentation that shows "how your methodology and your implementation map to each other" [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). It supports the Code of Practice for Statistics around quality assurance and transparency, and the authors share the code used to produce outputs wherever possible, "along with enough data to allow for proper testing" [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible").

### Auditable

If decisions rest on the analysis, the analysis and evidence must be available for scrutiny and audit; auditable analysis can at any point answer "Who made each decision?", "When was this decision made?" and "What evidence was this decision based on?" [V] (book/principles.md, "Auditable"). Answering them gives decision makers and users trust: they know the story of the analysis, who is responsible for each part, and what changes have been made [AP]. Code and data should be brought together and ideally published alongside reports with a record of analytical choices and their owners; reproducibility makes it easier for others to quality assure, assess and critique [AP] (book/principles.md, "Auditable").

### Assured

Analysis on which decisions are made must be held to high standards, in any medium including code, but some government analysis "doesn't bear on decisions at that level" and analysts should not be overburdened [AP] (book/principles.md, "Assured"). The government position is **proportionality**: "the right quality assurance procedures for the right analysis" [V], achieved through peer review and defensive design [AP] (book/principles.md, "Assured"). Readers should follow their department's guidance, most of which derives from the Aqua book [BT]; "Assurance is best demonstrated through peer review." [V]; reviewers must be able to understand the choices and reproduce the conclusions; dual running should be considered "particularly for high risk analysis" [V]; and guarantees of quality assurance should be published alongside any report [AP] (book/principles.md, "Assured").

### Reproducible analytical pipelines

Producing analysis such as official statistics can be time-consuming and painstaking; the aim is workflows that are "repeatable and sustainable over time" and follow reproducible-analysis principles, called RAP [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines"). "Reproducible analysis is still not widely practised across government." [V] Many analysts combine proprietary tools such as SAS or SPSS with Excel, Word or Acrobat in manual or semi-manual processes, and colleagues repeat parts manually to assure the outputs; this is time-consuming and error-prone, and can be frustrating, especially where manual steps are difficult to replicate quickly [AP] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines"). Open-source tools such as Python and R, coupled with Git and Git services, "have made it possible to develop automatic, streamlined processes, accompanied by a full audit trail" [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines"). RAP was first piloted in the Government Statistical Service in 2017 by analysts in DCMS and DfE working with GDS data scientists to automate statistical bulletins, and a network of RAP champions promotes and supports adoption across departments [AE] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines").

## Part III: Managing analytical code development

### Audience and starting points

This draft section targets those who manage data analysis, science and engineering work in government, or act as product owners for analytical products, and aims to help them support their teams to apply the book's practices [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Managing analytical code development"). Managers should have basic awareness of the tools and techniques (outlined by the introduction to RAP course) and of their department's platforms, and should use the Government Service Standard when designing and managing analysis as code [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Managing analytical code development").

### Apply quality assurance proportional to risk

Following the Aqua book, assurance should be proportionate to the complexity and risk the analysis carries [BT] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). A manager "should not need an in-depth understanding of the analysis code to trust that it is working correctly" [V], but should be confident the team took an appropriate approach for the user need and is applying proportionate assurance to development and running [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). Managers should decide with their team which practices each piece of analysis needs and, when possible, define the target assurance level before starting [AP].

An "important" box adds that team skills must be considered alongside risk: learning takes time, so managers should support gradual development, identify where each analyst is along the RAP learning pathway, and have them develop and apply "the next skill in the pathway" [V] "rather than attempting to adopt them all at once" [V]; maintaining technical skills in the team matters for sustainability [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk").

Despite the initial cost of skills, the section links to evidence (devops-research.com) that good practices increase the efficiency of development and the maintainability of code, and to case studies of improved government analysis [BT] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). Not following good practices creates technical debt, which slows further development; this "can be necessary for delivering to short deadlines" [V], but time should be set aside to address it [AP]. Where code assurance does not meet the target, "for example where there is limited time or skill" [V], managers should supplement it with more in-depth assurance of outputs, such as dual running with an independent system and consistency checks across output data [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk").

### Design quality analysis

Questions for the start of the analysis [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Design quality analysis"):

- *Why have you chosen to do the analysis this way?* Consult users at the beginning and throughout; methodology and data suited to the question; more than one person developing, to allow pair programming, peer review and mentoring, which "increases the sustainability of analysis" [V]; open-source tools wherever possible, with the team able to explain why its tools are fit for purpose [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Why have you chosen to do the analysis this way?").
- *How are you storing input data?* Version input data to reproduce outputs; store it in an open format (CSV or ODS), not formats restricted to proprietary software like SAS and Stata; put large or complex datasets in a database; monitor data quality using the government data quality framework [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How are you storing input data?").
- *How will you keep track of changes to the code and why they were made?* Version control the code, documentation and peer reviews; develop on an open-source code platform like GitHub, because "This transparency increases your users trust in the analysis and promotes collaboration and re-use." [V]; keep a record of every change and who made it, link each change to a reason, and store reviews with the version reviewed [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How will you keep track of changes to the code and why they were made?").

### Quality assure throughout development

Questions to assess progress towards the agreed target practices [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Quality assure throughout development"):

- *Code structure:* logic written as functions for consistent reuse and testing; related functions grouped in a file; logic with different responsibilities separated (reading versus transforming data); reusable code shared as a package [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How is your code structured?").
- *Adjusting runs:* parameters that often change between runs (input and output paths, reference dates, model parameters) kept in separate configuration files [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How easy is it to adjust the way that the analysis runs?").
- *Documentation:* code documentation "is essential for business continuity and sustainability" [V]; document every function, including inputs and outputs, with usage examples and test data where others will run or reuse the code [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How is the analysis documented?").
- *Dependencies:* user instructions; software and package versions recorded (`setup.py` and `requirements.txt`, or an R `DESCRIPTION` file); code not dependent on a specific computer, checked by running it on a colleague's system; reproducible outcomes across runs and systems; containers such as Docker [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "What are the dependencies?").
- *Assumptions:* recorded close to the code, and "You must communicate these to users when releasing results from the analysis." [V] (book/managers_guide.md, "What assumptions does the analysis make?").
- *Peer review:* internal review of each change by technical colleagues, which "will identify issues early on and makes the review process more manageable than reviewing only the final analysis" [V]; a standard procedure; evidence that reviews are acted on, with concerns addressed before the analysis is used; external review for high-risk products [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How has peer review been done?").
- *Testing:* testing means the code produces the right outputs for realistic example input; automated unit tests for each function; each function and the end-to-end analysis tested with minimal, realistic data; more extensive testing on the most important or complex parts, "However, ideally you would test every single function." [V]; realistic cases include missing data, zeroes, infinities, negative numbers, wrong types and invalid inputs; reviewers sign off that testing is enough; each identified error gets a test [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How have you tested the code?").
- *Failure:* informative error messages, helpful to another team operating the code; errors or warnings when data validation fails; errors logged in production [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "What happens when the analysis fails to run?").
- *Comparison with previous results:* large differences between repeated analyses may indicate a process issue; when replacing legacy analysis, running the two in parallel identifies differences and improvements [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How does the analysis result differ from the previous analysis?").
- *Further improvement:* "Code quality improves over time, as your team learn more about good practices." [V]; teams should aim at the agreed level while considering which practices to apply next, and managers should review training needs and allow time for development [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "How can we further improve the quality of the analysis?").

## Part IV: Writing code

### Modular code: motivation

The chapter adapts general programming principles to analytical workflows [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Modular code"). Even experienced programmers struggle with repetitive, disorganised or overly complex code, which makes assuring, testing and changing it more burdensome; non-modular code produces walls of repetition, long complex scripts, over-complicated code and a hard-to-search code base [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Motivation"). Modular code underpins the book's other practices (version control, review, testing, documentation), so "modular code is fundamental to making analysis more reproducible, auditable and assured" [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Motivation").

### Write re-usable code as functions

Early analysis often copies and pastes to "'make it work'" [V]; as code matures, repetitive code should become functions, which make logic reusable, consistent, readable and easier to test [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Write re-usable code as functions"). Signs that a function is too complex are that it is very long or needs many arguments; then break it into smaller functions and build a high-level function from them [AP]. The rule of thumb called 'referential transparency': "your code should run in the same way if a call to your function was replaced by the value that it would have returned" [V]. Functions should not depend on or affect variables not passed in as arguments, and the same inputs should always produce the same results; where side-effects are unavoidable (files, databases, external services) they should be documented for users and developers [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Write re-usable code as functions").

### Group data and methods as classes

Classes associate data (attributes) with logic (methods); because custom classes are less common in R, the section focuses on Python [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes"). The section covers:

- *Hiding state.* OOP can reduce complexity by hiding low-level details such as internal state (illustrated with a bank `Account` holding owner name, account number and balance); a leading underscore marks attributes and helper methods as 'private' by convention, though "In Python, the notion of 'private' does not mean secure." [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").
- *Duck typing.* What methods a class provides matters more than its type, illustrated with the saying "If it walks like a duck, and it quacks like a duck, then it must be a duck." [V] and a `LoyaltyAccount` that could stand in for a `BankAccount` [AE] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").
- *Inheritance and Liskov substitution.* Subclasses should extend without damaging the parent's functionality, so any `Account` can be replaced by a `BankAccount`; the same applies to functions that share an interface [BT] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").
- *Encapsulation over inheritance.* Inheritance locks a class to its superclass; to reuse code from an unrelated class (a `Car` using an `Engine`), keeping a private instance and delegating to it "may be more appropriate" [V] [AE] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").
- *Interfaces.* An interface specifies the methods a group of classes must provide; Python's `abc` abstract base classes achieve this, illustrated by a `FileHandler` with `CsvHandler` and `SqlHandler` subclasses, and by scikit-learn's linear models sharing `fit()` and `predict()` [AE] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").
- *Data Driven versus Responsibility Driven Design.* Mapping nouns in a system description to classes works for small systems but can leave one class holding most of the logic, which the book describes as 'Data Driven Design'; for more complex analytical work "a better approach might be" Responsibility Driven Design, with small, focused classes, while weighing the trade-off between one large class and many small ones [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes"). The worked example makes `Cheque` and `Cash` objects responsible for paying themselves in, so a bank account only holds, receives and pays out money [AE].
- *Law of Demeter.* Method chains such as `book.publisher().address().postcode()` are fragile; the 'Demeter' research project found this style produced a high proportion of bugs, giving "'Only talk to your immediate friends'" [V] [BT]; the fix adds methods, so "we're trading maintainability for complexity, so consider if it is worthwhile" [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").

The section's summary includes: classes hide implementation detail; use consistent methods across related classes; distribute logic by responsibility; beware one large class or too many; use Design Patterns as a toolbox; and "You should opt for encapsulation over inheritance, especially with code reuse." [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").

### Scripts, modules and packages

Scripts executed from the command line run top to bottom, in contrast to interactive interpreters or notebooks "where the human has control of the order of execution" [V]; manual line-by-line execution risks errors from wrong ordering, so the book recommends end-to-end scripts [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Split complex code into multiple scripts"). A note qualifies this: a script "does not guarantee that your code will run reproducibly, but it does ensure that code is run in the same way across multiple runs" [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Split complex code into multiple scripts").

Modules are scripts holding functions used by other scripts; the worked example splits one large analysis script into `processing`, `modelling` and `reporting` modules imported by a simple `main` script, with an R project file for relative paths [AE] (book/modular_code.md, "Organise related classes and functions into modules"). A warning says R projects save history and data by default, which risks data entering Git history, and shows how to turn this off [AP]. A note says the minimal main script cannot configure input paths, so users must edit paths in code, "which is highly discouraged" [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Organise related classes and functions into modules").

Useful, reusable solutions can be wrapped as packages for others to install; readers should ask whether their code solves a problem no one has solved in their language [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Organise and document your modules as packages"). Packaging properly applies many of the book's recommendations, and "it is not trivial to maintain and develop well-regarded open-source packages" [V]; applying the recommendations as you go makes final packaging simpler [AP] (book/modular_code.md, "Organise and document your modules as packages").

### Notebooks

Notebooks are hard to review and audit through version control because their internal format prevents line-by-line diffs in common tools; functions kept in notebooks are harder to test; and cells can run out of order, so "notebook results may not always be reproducible" [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Think carefully about whether notebooks are a suitable way to organise your code"). Their strengths are exploring data and presenting research code alongside a narrative, including as HTML reports [AP]. "In short, notebooks are not suitable for modularising analysis pipelines." [V] As exploration ends or the analysis must recur, notebooks should be refactored: repeated cells into functions, functions into modules, then documented and tested, with the pipeline run from a script [AP]. "Output generation should instead be trusted to scripts, where human decisions do not alter the order that code is run." [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Think carefully about whether notebooks are a suitable way to organise your code").

### Readable code: motivation and clean code

The chapter opens with an epigraph attributed to Guido van Rossum (creator of Python): "Code is read more often than it is written." [V] [BT] (book/readable_code.md, "Motivation"). Someone else will need to understand, use and adapt the code, and "That someone might be you in six months time!" [V]; empathising with them yields a 'self-documenting' codebase [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Motivation"). Readability is how easily another analyst gains a decent understanding of the code in reasonable time; maintainability is how easily others can understand it well enough to modify and repair it [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Motivation"). A Donald Knuth epigraph opens "Clean code"; clean code avoids confusion and ambiguity, and readers should consult their language's style guide "as first point of call" because those guides capture the most up-to-date guidance, which this document may not contain [V] [BT] (book/readable_code.md, "Clean code").

### Naming

"The most important aspect of clean code is the naming of identifiers within your code." [V]; names should be "informative and not misleading" and "concise but not cryptic" [V] (book/readable_code.md, "Use informative names"). For variables, avoid cryptic or single-letter names, except when implementing mathematical notation, where formulas must be clear, available and consistent and the source cited; a few (3 or so) informative words help; numerical suffixes such as `letters_1` and `letters_2` say nothing unless meaningful, while names can document differences and incremental changes; there is "a clear trade-off between the usability and informativeness of variable names" [V], more noticeable in Python, where indentation is syntax and PEP8 recommends line widths of 79 characters [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Give variables clear and concise names"). Function names should reveal purpose, typically starting with a verb, with question-form names for Boolean results; being unable to describe a function's task in a few words is a warning sign of over-complexity [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Name functions after the task that they perform"). A class too complex to name concisely indicates too many responsibilities and should be refactored into smaller classes [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Make classes easy to identify").

### Style and idiom

Style guides standardise layout across a language community, but teams have needs a general guide may not cover, so guides work best "as starting points in a discussion on 'how should our team be consistent internally in the way we write code?'" [V]; teams adopt or adapt them, with the goals of readability and consistency [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Make code easier to read by following a consistent style"). PEP8 is named for Python, and Google and tidyverse for R [AP]. The section's figure is the xkcd "Code Quality" comic (alt text: "Comic strip describing a brutal code review.") [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Make code easier to read by following a consistent style").

"There is perhaps a misconception that following style guidelines and formatting your code accordingly is the fundamental goal of writing good code in a given language." [V] Guidelines may lead reviews to focus on style over more fundamental problems; fluency includes writing idiomatic ('pythonic') code, shown by three equivalent Python and R loops of increasing idiom; yet "we should still prefer readability over idioms that might make our code more complex" [V] (book/readable_code.md, "Write code that other programmers will find easy to read"). Because checking style by hand is tedious, the book recommends automated support, cross-referring to linters and formatters [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Automate style checks").

### Software ideas for analysts

"It's important to remember that when we write code for analysis, we are developing software." [V] The section condenses software engineering practices for analysts and encourages reading further [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Software ideas for analysts").

- *Keep it simple.* Solve the problem with a clear outcome in mind; use existing packages rather than reinventing the wheel; split code into understandable parts; "Don't over-engineer your solution" [V]; pick one of several equivalent packages (dplyr or sqldf) and stick to it [AP]. A note says to capture requirements before writing code, warns that "many cases that you account for will never occur" [V], and quotes "You ain't gonna need it" [V]. Complex problems may need complex solutions; introduce complexity only where needed and address it with proportionate assurance through documentation, testing and review [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Keep it simple").
- *Don't repeat yourself.* Copy-pasted 'quick and dirty' code is natural early on, but if three copies exist and only two are fixed, "there is now a bug sleeping in the code waiting to be triggered" [V]; the worked example's third copy silently collects even numbers into `odd_third` [AE]. Modifying copies is "analogous to modifying the formula in individual cells of a spreadsheet" [V]. Refactoring into functions means fixes are made once; the 'Rule of Three' suggests extracting logic once similar code has been written more than two times, while anticipating reuse may justify writing it modularly from the start [AP] (book/readable_code.md, "Don't repeat yourself").
- *Be explicit.* Under the Zen of Python epigraph "Explicit is better than implicit" [V] [BT], the section shows that relying on the truthiness of `None`, `FALSE` or `0` can create a bug when a count of zero should print, and recommends stating the exact condition [AE] (book/readable_code.md, "Be explicit").
- *Separate responsibilities.* The single responsibility principle: a function or class "should take on one task and perform it well" [V], because code with fewer reasons to change is more robust [AP]. An economic `Country` class that grows unmanageable is broken into `UnemploymentModel` and `InflationModel`; 'separation of concerns' applies the idea at a higher level (low-level models, country and trade-block interactions, a `SimulationRunner`), with a `LoaderFactory` choosing data loaders; the same applies to function-based code [AE] (book/readable_code.md, "Separate responsibilities"). The section's figure is "Representation of concerns and responsibilities within a piece of software" [AP].
- *Open to extension, closed for modification.* Functionality should be extendable without modifying source code; the open-closed principle gives confidence that essential behaviour will not change and the ability to add functionality as code evolves [AP]. A note explains functional composition, "$h(x) = g(f(x))$", familiar from R's `%>%`, and extends a `report(model(load(filepath)))` pipeline with a `clean` step without touching `load` [AE] (book/readable_code.md, "Make functions open to extension, but closed for modification").

## Part V: Structuring and documenting projects

### Structuring your project

Analysis is exploratory and changeable, so scripts become messy; good directory structure and file hygiene mitigate this; some structures have proved effective "through trial and error", while others are specific and "should not be taken as mandatory" [V] (book/project_structure.md, "Structuring your project").

- *Run scripts end to end.* Saving working code in scripts (run in an IDE or from the command line) can be easier than running code in the console and rewriting it in a script later; running files end to end executes code in the same order each time and "with a clean environment, without variables or other objects from previous runs that can be a common source of errors" [V] (book/project_structure.md, "Run scripts from end to end to ensure your code is executed reproducibly").
- *Filename conventions.* "Consistency, above all else." [V]; short descriptive names; no spaces; consistent dates in YYYY-MM-DD form with the largest time unit first so files sort chronologically; zero-padded numbers; numeric prefixes where ordering is informative [AP] (book/project_structure.md, "Use good filename conventions").
- *Directed Acyclic Graph.* "Analysis can best be thought of as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)." [V]: input data at the start, outputs at the end, and "no lines that link backwards" [V]. Each project gets its own folder; most analysis has ingest, processing and reporting stages; folders separate raw data, documentation, source code and results; code shared across projects lives in its own folder [AP] (book/project_structure.md, "Organise analysis as a Directed Acyclic Graph").
- *Preserve raw data.* Treat raw data as read-only, clean a copy so cleaning decisions are documented, and keep an immutable raw-data store, often best kept apart from the code base [AP] (book/project_structure.md, "Preserve raw data").
- *Disposable outputs.* "If you are worried about deleting your outputs (i.e., results) then it is likely you lack confidence in reproducing your results." [V]; frequently deleting and regenerating outputs is good practice [AP] (book/project_structure.md, "Check that outputs are disposable").
- *Modules, packages, templates and repositories.* Complex, high-risk or reusable code can benefit from a package [AP] (book/project_structure.md, "Structure code as modules and packages"). Consistent structures help people orient in unfamiliar projects; Cookiecutter templates (govcookiecutter with data security features, cookiecutter-data-science, cookiecutter-pypackage), the RStudio package template, the hub's example R and Python packages, and R's `usethis` are named [AP] (book/project_structure.md, "Use project templates"). A version-controlled repository usually holds one project and "has significant benefits for reproducibility" [V] (book/project_structure.md, "Use version controlled repositories").

### Code documentation: comments

The chapter opens with Damian Conway's epigraph "Documentation is a love letter that you write to your future self." [V] [BT] (book/code_documentation.md, "Code documentation"). The comments section's guiding line is "Use comments sparingly and with purpose" [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments"). Comments explain non-obvious how and why; excessive comments create redundancy and can make code harder to read, and outdated comments mislead, because "the only point of 'truth' is the code that is executed" [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments"). Comments restating **what** the code does are usually unnecessary given good naming; needing many comments can signal code that should be refactored, though some complexity is real and "will eventually have to 'sit' somewhere" [V], so the key is to manage it without adding to it [AP]. Comments are most useful explaining **why** a choice was made [AP] (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments").

Commented-out code adds visual noise, and relying on someone to comment and uncomment code to change behaviour "is **highly discouraged**" [V]: it reduces reproducibility, raises the risk of deploying incorrect functionality, introduces a human factor, and lets dead code fall out of sync; control flow and configuration files should be used instead [AP] (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments").

### Docstrings and generated documentation

Docstrings are "the de facto way of documenting" functions and classes [V], kept close to the code so they are easier to keep current and available through `help(function_name)` [AP] (book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings"). They commonly describe what the code does, its parameters and types, what it returns, expected errors, the methodology implemented, example usage and related functions; the listed errors are only those the writer expects [AP] (book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings"). R documentation should use roxygen within packages [AP]. Writing descriptions before the code helps focus: "The documentation should be a specification of what the code is expected to do." [V] Docstrings must be kept up to date, or users may be misled, with consequences "ranging from wasted time to serious methodological implications or even outputs that are plain wrong" [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings"). Among styles (numpydoc, Google, PEP 257, roxygen2 with tidyverse), "the core idea behind style is **consistency**" [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings"). Modules and scripts get looser docstrings (title, description, usage notes, copyright, citations), illustrated with a "Duck census main analysis" script header [AE] (book/code_documentation.md, "Document scripts or modules using docstrings").

Accurate, accessible documentation "is one of the cornerstones of well-adopted, open-source packages" [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Generate documentation automatically"). Sphinx is recommended for Python, including its doctest extension, which runs docstring `Examples` and, though it "can't replace thorough code testing" [V], helps catch outdated documentation; pkgdown is suggested for R [AP] (book/code_documentation.md, "Python"; "R"). Built documentation should be hosted publicly, for example on GitHub Pages, where "The book that you're reading right now is hosted in this way." [V], or Read the Docs, and can be updated automatically through CI [AP] (book/code_documentation.md, "Make human readable documentation easily available to users").

### AI coding assistants (documentation)

An AI coding assistant asked to generate module and function documentation "can be very effective and can save you a lot of time" [V]; users should always check that the documentation is correct, clear and concise, and manage expectations "by providing well-defined, bounded requirements" [V]. "Do not expect a coding assistant to document your entire application correctly with minimal intervention." [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "AI coding assistants").

### Project documentation

- *README:* a short statement of intent, a description of the problem and solution, installation instructions, example usage, a screenshot for GUIs, and links to guidance and related projects [AP] (book/project_documentation.md, "README").
- *Contributing guidance:* standards, packages, code style, and a code of conduct where outside contributors are expected; the hub's gptables CONTRIBUTING file is the worked example, branching from `dev`, merging "once you have the sign-off of two maintainers" [V], using SemVer and numpydoc, and following a review process similar to rOpenSci's [AE] (book/project_documentation.md, "Contributing guidance").
- *User desk instructions:* for user-focused pipelines, how to set up the environment, configure, run, interpret outputs, what quality assurance "has been carried out and what further quality assurance of outputs is required" [V], and how to maintain the project [AP] (book/project_documentation.md, "User desk instructions").
- *Dependencies:* the environment includes machine, operating system, language and packages; record them (`requirements.txt`, `setup.py`, R `DESCRIPTION`) and use tools such as renv or pyenv [AP] (book/project_documentation.md, "Dependencies").
- *Citation and vignettes:* a `CITATION` file or README template, illustrated by ggplot2's; vignettes show several units working together in a realistic context [AE] (book/project_documentation.md, "Citation"; "Vignettes").
- *Versioning and changelog:* versioning combined with version control lets you "recover the exact code used to run your analysis, and thus reproduce the same results" [V]; Semantic Versioning signals API compatibility through major, minor and patch numbers (figure "Semantic versioning"); a Keep a Changelog example shows Added, Removed, Changed and Fixed entries [AP] (book/project_documentation.md, "Versioning"; "Changelog").
- *Copyright and licences:* material created by civil servants is Crown copyright; a notice is not essential but recommended in government projects; the Government Digital Service "generally recommends" the MIT licence for code and the Open Government Licence for documentation [V] [BT] (book/project_documentation.md, "Copyright and Licenses").
- *Open source your code:* government supports open source and "As a government analyst, you should aim to make all new source code open, unless you can justify witholding part of your source code." [V]; personal benefits are attribution, collaboration, review and that it "Feels good"; public benefits are transparency (a core element of the Statistics Code of Practice), sharing value and sharing opportunity [AP] (book/project_documentation.md, "Open source your code").

## Part VI: Version control, configuration and data

### Version control: audit trail and contents

Version control "is managing changes to your analysis over time" [V], with Git as the primary example (book/version_control.md, "Version control"). An audit trail answers what changed, when, why and who; Git records these through commits and Pull or Merge Requests, keeping the workspace clean of commented-out code and copies of old files (figure: the xkcd "Documents" comic on poor file naming) [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Keep an audit trail of changes"). A remote repository "maintains a single source of truth" [V], and platforms keep "review embedded in the development workflow" [V] (book/version_control.md, "Keep an audit trail of changes").

Repositories should include project and code documentation, unit tests, dummy data and example configuration, and user documentation [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Include code and documentation in version control"). A caution lists what should **never** be included: passwords, credentials or keys; real configuration files; code containing sensitive information (fraud-detection methods, references to personally identifiable data, security protocols); and data beyond small examples [AP]. Dummy data must not disclose sensitive features such as distributions and trends and "should always be carefully peer reviewed before being added to a repository" [V] (book/version_control.md, "Exclude sensitive information from version control").

### Using Git

- *Commits:* each is attributed to its author and identified by a hash; add files individually rather than with `git add .`; a model commit message (from "A note about Git commit messages") gives a summary of 50 characters or less, a body wrapped at about 72, and the imperative mood; commit whenever "a discrete unit of work has been completed" [V], and keep each commit to a single aspect so a revert does not also remove unrelated changes [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Write short and informative commits").
- *Branching:* branching "should be proportional to number of collaborators and the complexity of the development work" [V]; `main` is the most stable branch, changes are made on branches and merged once reviewed and tested; GitHub flow uses Pull Requests to bring peer review into the workflow; independent features avoid conflicts; deeper branches serve sub-tasks and fixes; Git flow's `develop` branch suits deploying to production from `main`, but "analysts should use the most simple and beneficial approach to branching depending on their project" [V]; branch names should be informative, ideally with issue numbers [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Use branching appropriately"). The section carries five branching figures, listed in the structure block.
- *Merge conflicts:* resolved manually; avoided by not editing the same files on different branches, and hard-to-avoid conflicts may mean scripts "are too monolithic and should be modularised" [V] (book/version_control.md, "Resolve merge conflicts").
- *Large files:* large or binary files bloat history and slow cloning, pushing and CI; Git LFS stores pointers instead, and git-annex is an alternative; even so, "we recommend that remote Git repositories are not used to store data" [V], and data versioning should be independent of code, for example with DVC or third-party storage [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Versioning large files").
- *Tags:* commit hashes "serve as really poor identifiers for human users" [V]; annotated tags mark model versions, important stages, or code used for a particular output so it can be recovered [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Tag new releases").

### Avoid committing sensitive information

"Code itself is very rarely sensitive, so we should be open to sharing it." [V] Credentials and personally identifiable data are the risks; credentials belong in environment variables, not code, "This includes in the early stages of development, as your version control history will retain copies of these." [V] (book/version_control.md, "Avoid committing sensitive information to Git repositories").

- `.gitignore` patterns exclude files and folders, but already-tracked files are not excluded by new patterns, so set it up first; dummy examples of excluded files help reuse [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Automatically avoid committing unwanted files using .gitignore").
- R's `.RData` and `.Rhistory` can capture sensitive data or commands; exclude them or, safest, stop R generating them [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Exclude `.Rdata` and `.Rhistory` files").
- Jupyter notebooks store the data behind cell outputs by default; since this cannot currently be prevented, clear outputs before committing, automated with a Git filter defined in `.gitattributes` and `.gitconfig` (an approach borrowed from a blog post by Yury Zhauniarovich) [AP] [BT] (book/version_control.md, "Avoid saving data from Jupyter Notebooks").
- Repository visibility and GitHub Organizations and Teams can limit access, but "Access control should not be used instead of the good practices outlined above." [V] (book/version_control.md, "Control access to code only when essential").
- The book calls it a data breach if unauthorised individuals may access sensitive information accidentally included in a remote repository; handle it by first preventing further access (restrict the repository, remove files from the **commit history**, change exposed credentials, have holders re-clone) and second reporting it (estimate exposure and impact, inform the data owner, discuss with the Data Protection Officer, and report pre-publication statistics breaches to the Office for Statistics Regulation) [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Handle data breaches via Git"). A warning: "Deleting a sensitive file and committing this change is not sufficient." [V]; the history must be rewritten, for example with git-filter-repo or BFG [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Handle data breaches via Git").

### Using GitHub

GitHub is described as "the world's leading software development platform" [V] (book/version_control.md, "Using GitHub"). Issues act as a collaborative to-do list, combine with project boards, reference other issues and people, and with templates encourage informative bug reports and feature requests; public issues let users say which changes would help them most [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Use Git issues to plan and discuss development of your project"). Pull Requests merge a source branch onto a more stable target, link issues (closing them with keywords such as 'fixes #42'), carry checklists for authors and reviewers, and offer a "Files changed" view for line comments and suggested changes (figure from a `fingertipsR` Pull Request) [AP]. A note advises considering preventing merges onto the `main` branch "without an approved Pull Request to enforce peer review" [V], combined with a Pull Request template [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Use pull requests for reviewing changes"). Forks serve external contribution or independent adaptation and do not synchronise automatically [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Fork a repository to maintain an independent copy"). Project boards, GitHub Pages and wikis are noted, and CI is deferred to its own chapter [AP] (book/version_control.md, "Use GitHub Actions for continous integration"; "Other GitHub features").

### Configuration

"Configuration describes how your code runs when you execute it." [V]; the chapter shows how to define configuration that is easy to update and separate from analysis logic, so others can run the code on other machines [AP] (book/configuration.md, "Configuration"). Configuration should hold high-level parameters such as file paths, database connection settings and model parameters [AP] (book/configuration.md, "Basic configuration"). The worked example begins with hard-coded machine-specific paths and two prediction lines switched by commenting, a practice to avoid because "another analyst would not be sure which set of parameters was used to produce a given set of predictions" [V] [AE]; it then gathers parameters into an in-code configuration section [AE]. Configuration should stay simple; include things that depend on the computer or change between runs [AP] (book/configuration.md, "Basic configuration").

Separate configuration files let code be version controlled on logic changes alone while a separate record shows which configuration produced which results; machine-specific or sensitive configuration may stay out of version control, with an up-to-date example file in its place [AP] (book/configuration.md, "Use separate configuration files"). Configuration can be a code file imported or `source()`d, or a dedicated format such as YAML, TOML, JSON or XML; formats like YAML and TOML are "compact and human-readable" [V] (book/configuration.md, "Use code files for configuration"; "Use dedicated configuration files"). Passing the configuration file path as a command-line argument removes the hard-coded path; options could be passed directly instead, "However, you should use configuration files as they allow us to document which configuration has been used to produce our analysis outputs, for reproducibility." [V] (book/configuration.md, "Use configuration files as arguments"). Credentials should never be written in code; configuration files risk being committed, so store secrets in environment variables, read with `os.environ.get` or `Sys.getenv` [AP] (book/configuration.md, "Configure secrets as environment variables").

### Data management

Analysts often manage their own data or work alongside data professionals; reproducing an analysis requires identifying and accessing the same data, which needs suitable storage, documentation and versioning [AP] (book/data.md, "Data management"). A "Key strategies" box calls the Government Data Quality Framework "a primary resource for all analysts working with data in the public sector" [V] and points to the Office for Statistics Regulation's standard for quality assurance of administrative data [BT] (book/data.md, "Data management").

- *Storage:* use open or standard formats for long-term storage and avoid formats that depend on SPSS, STATA or SAS [AP] (book/data.md, "Data storage").
- *Spreadsheets:* their flexibility comes at the cost of harder quality assurance (figure: the xkcd ".NORM Normal File Format" comic); "Do not use spreadsheets for storage of data (or statistics production and modelling processes)." [V], because of "Lack of audibility" [V], multi-user clashes, error-proneness with no built-in quality assurance, unwieldy large files and silent automatic 'correction' of dates and data types; the European Spreadsheet Risks Interest Group's document on spreadsheet-related errors and their consequences is cited [AP] [BT] (book/data.md, "Spreadsheets").
- *Databases:* DBMSs usually support authorisation of database access and concurrent access by multiple users; open-source examples are SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL and Redis; relational databases link tables through keys; ORMs are user-friendly but may not support all SQL; good practices are auto-generated primary keys, logical tables to reduce redundancy, and locking tables that should not change [AP] (book/data.md, "Databases").
- *Documenting data:* analysts need to know what data exist, how they were collected, how they are represented, whether they have been validated or manipulated, and how they may ethically and legally be used [AP] (book/data.md, "Documenting data"); a data dictionary describes each variable's meaning, frame of reference, labels or valid ranges, missing-data representation, derivation and usage rules, with the NHS National Workforce Data Set as an example [AE] (book/data.md, "Data dictionary"); an Information Asset Register records dataset owners, descriptions, reasons for holding, storage and security, and loss risk [AP] (book/data.md, "Information Asset Register (IAR)").
- *Version control data:* open and secondary data may be revised or vanish without notice, and owners cannot be relied on for history; "As an analyst, it is your responsibility to ensure you identify the exact data that you have used." [V] Version and document every change with its reason; treat reproducible outputs as disposable or else version them against inputs and code; DVC and `daff` can help; manual versions need unique names, must be read-only, and modifications create new versions; record which data version produced which outputs [AP] (book/data.md, "Version control data").
- *Publishing:* the 5-star open data standards, CSV on the Web (recommended "for achieving the highest ratings of open data" [V]), the releasing-statistics-in-spreadsheets guidance and the GOV.UK Tabular data standard [AP] (book/data.md, "Use these standards and guidance when publishing data").

## Part VII: Assurance practices

### Peer review: purpose and proportion

Peer review of code is "a quality assurance activity where a developer, other than the code's author, views and tests the usage of a piece of code" [V]; it brings fresh eyes, assures the approach, may highlight errors, improves quality and gives confidence that the analysis is fit for purpose [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review"). Two epigraphs frame the chapter: one from the Aqua book on assessing utility, reliability and validation, and one attributed to "Nick Macphereson, former Permanent Secretary to the Treasury" on continuous challenge and public trust [V] [BT] (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review"). Following the Aqua book, review should be proportionate to complexity and business risk; external review is recommended "if your analysis uses novel or complex techniques, if comparison with other analyses cannot be used to challenge your results, or if the analysis is business critical" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review").

### What reviews focus on

"Reviewing is centered around conversations" [V]; example questions for reviewers [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "Focus reviews on code quality"):

- *Can I easily understand what the code does?* Documentation, duplication and simple functions; reviewers challenge constructively, and internal review transfers knowledge in both directions because the reviewer "must understand what the code is doing to validate that it works as expected" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Can I easily understand what the code does?").
- *Is the required functionality tested sufficiently?* Reviewers ask "whether the amount of testing is proportionate given the risk to the analysis if the code does not work" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Is the required functionality tested sufficiently?").
- *How easy will it be to alter this code when requirements change?* Parameters in configuration files rather than manual edits through the code, which "is much more risky" [V]; continued assessment of whether the analysis meets customer needs, supported by documented scope and requirements, assumption logs, technical reports and verification records [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "How easy will it be to alter this code when requirements change?").
- *Can I generate the same outputs that the analysis claims to produce?* Documented dependencies and recorded code version, input data version and configuration; "Assurance that analysis can be reproduced increases the trust in the results." [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Can I generate the same outputs that the analysis claims to produce?").

These questions focus "on important quality assurance practices in the code, rather than minor issues like code layout and style" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Can I generate the same outputs that the analysis claims to produce?").

### Giving feedback

Feedback should be practical, constructive and impersonal; the CEDAR model structures it as Context, Examples, Diagnosis, Actions and Review, and "has been designed from a coaching or mentoring perspective" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Give practical feedback"). Developers either justify their approach or act on feedback before the analysis is used; reviewers may re-review; and an "important" box says to document what was considered and how the developer responded, kept close to the code version, most easily through Merge or Pull Requests [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "Document review feedback and outcomes"). A Markdown review template covers documentation, installation, functionality, automated tests and packaging guidelines, then detailed comments, closing "Be critical and clear, but not mean. Ask questions and set actions." [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Give consistent feedback").

### Timeliness: pair programming and separate review

Feedback should be timely so review does not hold up development and issues are fixed before more code repeats them; "We strongly recommend applying pair programming for code review, as the most timely and practical method." [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Give timely feedback"). In pair programming two or three developers take turns authoring while others give real-time feedback, "programming out loud"; it can be more efficient than separate review, and "Despite the upfront cost of two individuals writing the code, the resulting code is often higher quality and contains fewer bugs." [V]; rotation spreads knowledge and reduces risk on individuals, and key discussions should still be documented [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "Review through pair programming").

Separate review works best with small, frequent changes [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary"). An "important" box: "If a project is only reviewed when all of the code has been written, this significantly reduces the benefit of review." [V]; late review burdens the reviewer and makes retrofitting documentation and testing costly [AP]. Large reviews can be split into sessions by aspect, and expecting review encourages clear code and usable dependency management from the outset [AP] (book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary"). A case study follows rOpenSci's open GitHub review of Public Health England's `fingertipsR` package: a submission checked against minimum requirements and the `goodpractice` package, CI reports saving reviewer time, two external reviews whose "detailed bespoke comments" [V] were perhaps the most informative part, author responses, and sign-off; parts of the process can be applied to smaller code [AE] (book/peer_review.md, "Case study - rOpenSci review").

### Testing: purpose and what to test

"You cannot confirm your code works correctly if you don’t carry out tests, so you cannot be confident that your analysis is fit for purpose without them." [V] "Good tests tell a story - given this data, having run this code, we expect this output." [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Testing code"). The question is "How can I demonstrate that my code does what it is supposed to do?" [V], and the developer is best placed to answer it [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "What should I test?"). Testing should be risk-based and proportionate, usually with more tests for very new, complex or risky code [AP]. Four considerations: you do not need to test adequately assured third-party tools (base R, CRAN packages), though very new or experimental tools may need validation; check that third-party tools do what your context needs (base R `round()` "intentionally behaves differently" to Excel's rounding [V]); thinking about tests challenges your own assumptions; and let the risks to mitigate guide what you test [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "What should I test?").

### Test structure and test discipline

Tests usually follow Arrange, Act, Assert; the section assumes a framework (`pytest`, `testthat`) and code in a package, since testing unpackaged code is harder [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "How are tests structured?").

- *Reproducible:* informal checks on example data should be turned into code tests so anyone can repeat them; test code follows the book's other practices [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Write reproducible tests").
- *Repeatable:* tests must be independent with no shared state (randomising order encourages this), deterministic where possible so "the only reason for a test to fail should be that the code being tested is incorrect" [V], with fixed random seeds or, where that is not possible, assertions about a distribution of outcomes (a coin flip run 100 times) [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Write repeatable tests").
- *Run all tests on every change:* this catches unexpected side-effects; failures after changed functionality remind you to update tests and documentation; CI automates the running [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Run all tests against each change to your code").
- *Record outcomes:* for auditability, record test outcomes with the code version, most simply through CI on the version control platform [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Record the outcomes of your tests").
- *Minimal test data:* "only just detailed enough", "fake, static (hardcoded), and readable", "stored closely to the test" [V]. A warning: "You must not copy the output from running your code to create your expected test outcomes." [V], because that assumes the function already works; "You must create your test data independently, ensuring that it reflects how you want your code to work, rather than how it currently works." [V] The worked example replaces a sales table with columns for 30 regions by four rows of two generic inputs covering positive, negative and zero values, which clarifies the test, avoids disclosure, and pushes the function towards generic, reusable parameters [AE] (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data").
- *Structure:* mirror the code's structure in test files (one per function, class or module), with unit, integration and end-to-end folders in the Python example and one `testthat` file per function in R; group Python tests in classes, noting inheritance makes tests easier to mix up; move tests out of package code when packaging; follow PEP8 or Google/tidyverse layout, install the package in editable mode, and order tests as the functions are ordered [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Structure test files to match code structure"; "Structuring tests").

### Unit, integration and end-to-end tests

- *Unit tests:* a unit is "the smallest modular piece of logic in the code - a function or method" [V]; cover boundary cases, positive, negative, zero and missing inputs, and examples that trigger defined errors; documented expected inputs reduce the need to test unexpected cases, and likely or risky misuse should raise an error; reused logic from already-tested packages needs no tests when used alone, but newly developed or little-used packages "are more likely to not be thoroughly tested" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Test that new logic is correct using unit tests").
- *Integration tests:* test multiple units, pipeline stages, and typical inputs from other systems; they give assurance the analysis is fit for purpose and safety when refactoring, illustrated by an imputation stage; a note says they "are more robust when they focus on general high level outcomes that you don't expect to change often" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Test that different parts of the code interact correctly using integration tests").
- *End-to-end tests:* also called system testing; check the whole workflow, including a "regression" test on exact output values, run in an environment close to production; because they are 'black box' tests, they should be used alongside unit tests [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Test that the analysis runs as expected using end-to-end tests").
- *Good practices:* plan ahead, test early, use real data where possible or data reflecting its complexity, automate, check dependencies between components, test failures as well as success, isolate tests, and document results [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Good practices for integration and end-to-end testing").

### Isolating tests from external systems

Tests that touch production databases risk data damage and real API calls can incur costs; isolating external systems lets tests evaluate how the code handles a response, not the dependency, and shows whether errors come from the system or the code (the unit under test is the 'System Under Test') [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Isolate code tests from external systems"). Mocking replaces `requests.get()` with a `Mock()`; the example code block opens with the comment "# AI has been used to produce content within this artefact." [V] [AE]. Because a broken mock could let a real request run while tests still pass, better practice asserts the mock was called and matches error messages with `pytest.raises()`; fixtures can generate mock attributes, with `Mock.reset_mock()` between cases, and pytest's monkeypatching is an alternative [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Isolate code tests from external systems").

### Bugs, TDD and the cost of skipping tests

Each bug should get a new test, which keeps fixed bugs from reappearing and "increases the coverage of your tests in a proportionate way" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests to assure that bugs are fixed"). "The best practice for testing code is to use test-driven development (TDD)." [V]: because the desired outcome is known in advance (from a user need or an internal requirement), the test can be written first; TDD repeats Red, Green, Refactor, starting from minimum functionality and growing complexity while refactoring manages it [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic"). TDD also encourages minimal test data and focused functions, and the section states "TDD requires practice but is proven to produce clean, robust and adaptable code." [V]; behaviour-driven and acceptance-test-driven development are named as extensions focused on user needs [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic").

A closing section concedes that skipping tests may sometimes be necessary (tight deadlines, limited resources, getting a feature running), warns it can hide problems that grow harder to fix as the project grows, and advises "Whenever tests are set aside, it’s best to have a plan for going back to add them" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "In a time crunch? The risks to skipping tests").

### Modelling-relevant testing

Model tests should use representative, unbiased, diverse data that is updated regularly [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Modelling-relevant testing"). The section names acceptance testing in three types (User, Business and Operational Acceptance Testing); goal-aligned metrics, such as precision and recall for data linkage; k-fold cross-validation to detect overfitting; stress testing with extreme or noisy inputs; sensitivity analysis of inputs and parameters; interpretability methods such as SHAP and LIME "for building trust with stakeholders" [V]; and optimisation such as grid search and parameter tuning [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Acceptance testing"; "Defining and Using Appropriate Metrics"; "Cross-Validation Techniques"; "Stress Testing"; "Sensitivity Analysis"; "Model Interpretability"; "Model Optimisation").

### Reducing repetition in tests; testing SQL

"Tests are code too" [V], so repetition should be reduced, though "You can be more tolerant of repetition in test code." [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Reduce repetition in test code (fixtures and parameterised tests)"; "Use fixtures to reduce repetition in test set up"). Fixtures define setup and clean-up once, scoped per test, group or session: a session-scoped `SparkSession` (safe only if no test modifies it) and a function-scoped test database reset between tests [AE] (book/testing_code.md, "Use fixtures to reduce repetition in test set up"). Parameterisation is "equivalent to using a for-loop" over inputs and expected outputs, done with `pytest.mark.parametrize` or R's `patrick`; a `sum_two_nums` example runs three simple parameterised tests, then stacks two parametrize marks with an expected-answers fixture to run 25 combinations [AE] (book/testing_code.md, "Use parameterisation to reduce repetition in test logic"; "Define Source Code"; "Simple Parameterisation"; "Stacked Parameterisation"). SQL testing is "outside the scope of this guidance" [V], but long queries can be broken up, tested in development rather than production databases, and checked with frameworks such as tSQLt and pgTAP [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Testing SQL").

### Automating code quality assurance

"Automating the running of unit tests is especially important to establish trust in your pipeline or package, by ensuring that all unit tests pass before every merge." [V] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Motivation"). Because running tests by hand is easy to forget, tests and other checks can trigger on changes to the remote repository, and reviewers can see the results [AP] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Automate tests to reduce risk of errors").

Committing small changes regularly "is often referred to as Continuous Integration (CI)" [V]: commit every working change ("Fixed a typo? Commit." [V]), a few times an hour as a rough guide, push at least daily, and, if a task is unfinished at day's end, consider whether it was broken down enough; CI should be underpinned by automated checks that the code builds or installs and its tests pass [AP] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Commit small changes often"). Git hooks such as `pre-commit` or `pre-push` can run tests, style checks or commit standards and stop a failing commit or push; tox, nox and rhub test across versions [AP] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Use Git hooks to encourage good practice"). Linters flag stylistic errors (and sometimes bugs or security issues); formatters also correct the formatting; the table names `flake8`, `pylint`, `Bandit`, `Black` and `Isort` for Python, `lintr`, `formatR` and `styler` for R, and `pymarkdownlnt` for Markdown; users should read each tool's documentation and may combine several [AP] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Linters and formatters").

GitHub Actions and GitLab Pipelines define workflows in YAML that build and test on every push [AP] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Workflows"). The example workflow runs on pushes to `master` and on every Pull Request, reports results on the request's page where a failure "can block the merge" [V], and repeats across four Python versions on Ubuntu [AE] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Configure GitHub actions to automate tests"). Documentation builds are illustrated by this book's own workflow and govcookiecutter's [AE] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Configure GitHub actions to build and deploy documentation"); GitLab Pipelines are "practically the same, with a change in syntax and file structure" [V] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Example GitLab Pipeline"). The `jupyter-book` project's CI is the comprehensive example: pre-commit style checks, tests over Python versions, `sphinx` versions and operating systems, coverage reporting, documentation builds and deployment to PyPI [AE] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Comprehensive example of automating code quality assurance").

## Part VIII: Generative AI

### Framing of the chapter

The chapter, illustrated by "A conversation with an Artifical Intelligence?" and flagged as a work in progress, notes that generative AI "has become the most talked-about technological development in recent years" [V] and that "Most of us have heard the confident assertion that the use of generative AI as a coding assistant will revolutionise how coders work." [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Generative AI"). It sets out to explain the underlying technology and suggest how to get the most from the tools, and supplements the Government Playbook on AI, "all the principles laid out in the playbook still apply here" [V] [BT] (book/generative_ai.md, "Generative AI").

### Machine learning and LLMs

Generative AI is a class of machine learning models, software "trained on a set of data to make predictions when given new data" [V]; government analysts may already know machine learning [AP] (book/generative_ai.md, "Introduction - Machine learning and Large Language Models"). A dropdown primer explains linear regression as $y' = b + m_1x_1$, with label, feature, bias and weight, training on labelled data, L2 loss, mean squared error and gradient descent until the model has **converged**, illustrated by "Gradient descent in supervised learning. Credit: Google" [AE] (book/generative_ai.md, "Machine learning rapid primer - linear regression").

Generative models' predictions are novel text, images, video or audio; the chapter focuses on LLMs, typically text-to-text, naming OpenAI's GPT series, Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude and DeepSeek [AP] (book/generative_ai.md, "Introduction - Machine learning and Large Language Models"). "The simplest way of putting it is that LLMs are next-word-predictor machines." [V], able to produce text that 'looks right' because they have learned a mathematical pattern for human text using a neural network [AP]. The chapter explains neurons, input and hidden layers, weights, biases and activation functions (the rectified linear unit, $f(x) = max(0, x)$), without which networks cannot learn non-linearity (figure: a neural network diagram credited to Wolfram Research) [AP]. Deep networks can learn patterns without being told what they are (a car-versus-bicycle classifier), trained by gradient descent implemented as backpropagation (figure credited to Stephen Wolfram) [AP] (book/generative_ai.md, "Introduction - Machine learning and Large Language Models").

"LLMs are essentially just very large neural networks." [V]; trained on vast text, they assign probabilities to words in sequences, but "a trained LLM is a black box" [V]: with billions if not trillions of terms, "nobody can say for sure why it is capable of such accurate mimicry, we can only assess that it is" [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Introduction - Machine learning and Large Language Models").
