The chapter attributes LLMs' spread to the transformer architecture, "invented in 2017 at Google" [V] for machine translation, which allowed 'hyperscaling', where larger networks and training data led to predictable performance gains [BT]; post-training ('fine-tuning'), a kind of reinforcement learning from human feedback, varies by company, in many cases involves "substantial human labour" [V] [BT], and is "increasingly important in the field of LLMs" [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Introduction - Machine learning and Large Language Models").

### Vibe coding, hallucinations and the golden rules

Many programmers have opted, or been instructed, to use LLMs to generate code on the logic "that it is faster to write prompts to generate code than it is to hand write code" [V]; "The slang term for this working practice is 'vibe coding'." [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"). LLMs "can and regularly do generate **plausible but inaccurate** statements" [V], and their production is "mathematically inevitable" [V], citing an arXiv paper [BT]. "This is not an example of the models 'failing', it is a feature" [V]: "Outputs that 'look right' are all that the models are trained to produce." [V], and "LLMs do not have an internal world-model of what is true and false" [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace").

From this the chapter derives three golden rules, set as "important" admonitions [AR] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"):

1. "You must never use or submit to peer review any code generated by an LLM without first reviewing it yourself." [V]
2. Derived from the first: "The only person responsible for the code you generated with an LLM is you." [V]
3. On inputs, since a chatbot is also a website: "Treat the input of an LLM chatbot as you would any other public online domain. Under no circumstances should you enter sensitive information or data in the input of an LLM chatbot." [V]

### Benefits and risks

*Benefits.* "The most touted advantage of vibe coding is a significant increase in productivity." [V] LLMs can generate code from expressions up to modules; IDE integration (VS Code with GitHub CoPilot) lets them modify files directly; vibe coding can free teams from menial tasks and "empower individuals to tackle more ambitious tasks than they would otherwise be comfortable with" [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Don't kill my vibe - The benefits of vibe coding"). One study across Microsoft and Accenture found "experimental evidence" that AI-assisted programmers write code faster: a statistically significant increase in pull requests and builds, "However, there was no overall statistically significant difference in the number of *successful* builds between the two groups." [V] [BT] (book/generative_ai.md, "Don't kill my vibe - The benefits of vibe coding").

*Risks.* In practice users "will inevitably be forced to spend a substantial amount of re-prompting, reviewing, and editing the outputs of LLMs" [V]; an AI-assisted programmer may become "a full time code reviewer for their LLM assistant" [V], with total task time unchanged or higher [AP] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe check failed - The risks of vibe coding"). METR researchers found that experienced AI-assisted programmers took longer than non-AI-assisted ones yet believed they had been more efficient; the study's authors proposed five potential explanations: complacency from overoptimism, lack of domain-specific knowledge, worse performance in large and complex codebases, high rejection of outputs with much time spent reviewing and editing, and missing implicit project context [BT] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe check failed - The risks of vibe coding"). A study by Anthropic "suggests that LLM adoption, especially if it is done quickly and aggressively, can have a negative impact on individuals' ability to learn on the job" [V] [BT]. The chapter draws potentially serious organisational implications for internal career progression and technical debt within teams [AR]. It also cites measured negative impacts on psychological wellbeing after LLM adoption in the workplace (increased boredom, decreased motivation), and a risk that LLM-generated code can contain critical security vulnerabilities, of particular importance to web-based platforms and applications [BT]. The chapter adds its own environmental concerns (vast electricity and fresh-water consumption, especially in training) and ethical concerns (copyrighted works in training data, reproduced bias, offensive and harmful content) [AP] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe check failed - The risks of vibe coding").

### Centaurs and reverse-centaurs

Drawing on Cory Doctorow, a centaur is a human assisted by a machine, which takes the drudgery out of work; a reverse-centaur is a human who assists a machine and is "stripped of agency in your work - the machine dictates what you do and when you do it" [V] [BT]. "When we use AI tools at work, we want to be centaurs and we don't want to be reverse-centaurs." [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs").

The worked example asks CoPilot for a function to flag outliers in a data pipeline [AE]. The first prompt appears only as an image, "A prompt offloading most of the thinking to CoPilot."; because it was vague and asked for 'quality standards' "(rather than verifying that by yourself!)" [V], CoPilot returned "a verbose, defensively-coded response" [V]: one class containing only attributes, five functions, 225 new lines, and an import of `__future__` "that suggests there could be compatibility issues in the code" [V], "practically the size of an entire pull request" [V] to review, so the user may turn into a reverse-centaur who must test and review code CoPilot designed and wrote [AE] (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs"). The updated prompt, again only an image ("An updated prompt where I am more precise with my requirements."), specified numerical data in pandas DataFrames and the thresholding; CoPilot returned one function of 46 lines importing only numpy and pandas: "You get to design the code, while CoPilot is doing the menial work of typing it up." [V] [AE] (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs").

The general principle: "LLM-powered chatbots are most useful when you direct them to work for you, rather than when you are picking up after them and trying to shape their outputs into something functional." [V] They "have no world-model of what is right and wrong", lack "any innate understanding of the requirements for your work", and "can't be held responsible for shoddy work" [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs"). The acknowledgements credit Stephen Wolfram's "What Is ChatGPT Doing ... and Why Does It Work" as having "informed much of the first section" and the Google Machine Learning Crash Course [V] [BT] (book/generative_ai.md, "Acknowledgements").

## Part IX: Supporting material

### Learning resources

The page links training and self-led resources, many on the UK Statistics Authority Learning Hub, available to all government analysts on request [AP] (book/learning.md, "Learning resources"). Non-government providers "may not always follow best practice", though exposure to applied examples still helps, and learners should compare what they learn with the guidance [V] (book/learning.md, "Learning resources"). Resources are grouped under core programming (the RAP learning pathway first), data manipulation, command line tools, Git, testing, accessibility and RAP, ending with "Learning from mistakes" and *The Little Book of Python Anti-Patterns* [AP] (book/learning.md, "Core programming"; "Learning from mistakes").

### Tools

The page lists tools supporting reproducible analysis, marking those developed or contributed to within government "(gov)", invites additions by issue, email or Pull Request, and cautions that listed tools may still contain bugs or limitations, so "Please apply your own judgement when using them." [V] (book/tools.md, "Tools"). Categories are data manipulation (pandas, Polars, PySpark, Splink (gov), dplyr, sparklyr); publishing (afcolours (gov), Quarto, a11ytables (gov), gptables (gov)); testing (pytest, unittest, hypothesis, chispa, coverage; testthat, assertr, patrick, covr); dependency management (venv, pyenv, renv, conda); version control (Git, pre-commit); project templates (govcookiecutter and Rgovcookiecutter, both (gov)); linters (pylint, flake8, Bandit, mypy, Radon; lintr); formatters (Black, Isort; formatR, styler); packaging (twine; goodpractice, fusen); pipeline orchestration (Apache Airflow, targets); and CI platforms (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Travis, Jenkins, Coveralls) [AP] (book/tools.md, "Data manipulation and analysis" through "Continuous Integration Platforms").

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Proprietary analysis software for reproducible work.* SAS, SPSS and Stata are "expensive to use and do not support many of the good analysis practices outlined in this guidance" [V], and data formats tied to them should be avoided (book/glossary.md, "Open source"; book/managers_guide.md, "How are you storing input data?"; book/data.md, "Data storage").
- *Manual and semi-manual production processes.* Framed as time-consuming and error-prone because inputs and outputs connect only through manual intervention; such processes can be frustrating, especially where manual steps are difficult to replicate quickly [AP] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines").
- *Spreadsheets for data storage, statistics production and modelling.* "Do not use spreadsheets for storage of data (or statistics production and modelling processes)." [V] (book/data.md, "Spreadsheets").
- *Notebooks as the means of producing outputs.* "In short, notebooks are not suitable for modularising analysis pipelines." [V]; they "should not be used as the main method of actually generating outputs" [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Think carefully about whether notebooks are a suitable way to organise your code").
- *Switching behaviour by commenting code in and out.* "**highly discouraged**" [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments"; book/configuration.md, "Basic configuration").
- *Style compliance as the goal of good code.* Named "perhaps a misconception" [V] (book/readable_code.md, "Write code that other programmers will find easy to read").
- *Data Driven Design and inheritance for reuse.* Responsibility Driven Design "might" be better for complex work, and "You should opt for encapsulation over inheritance, especially with code reuse." [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Group data and methods as classes").
- *Expected test outputs copied from the code's own output.* "You must not copy the output from running your code to create your expected test outcomes." [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data").
- *Review only at the end.* "this significantly reduces the benefit of review" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary").
- *Access control as a substitute for good version-control practice, and deletion as a breach fix.* "Access control should not be used instead of the good practices outlined above." [V]; "Deleting a sensitive file and committing this change is not sufficient." [V] (book/version_control.md, "Control access to code only when essential"; "Handle data breaches via Git").
- *Using LLM-generated code unreviewed, and offloading the design to the model.* The first golden rule forbids using or submitting unreviewed LLM code [AP]; vague prompting that offloads "too much of the cognitive work" [V] can turn the user into a reverse-centaur (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"; "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs").
